about: Taiwanese clinical-stage biotech developing silmitasertib (CX-4945), a casein kinase 2 inhibitor tested in cholangiocarcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and COVID-19, plus research on kinase inhibitors. Listed on the Taiwan emerging stock market. Pre-revenue. Specialist drug developer with no consumer brand. The firm's drug was discovered at a US biotech and developed in Taiwan, where it is one of the more advanced local oncology programmes.

Seoul genetic diagnostics company that uses AI-based variant interpretation to diagnose rare genetic diseases from sequencing data, serving clinicians and labs in Korea and abroad, with the EVIDENCE software and its own testing services. Listed on KOSDAQ. Customers are hospitals and patients. Specialist B2B health brand with little public awareness. Its customers include geneticists, children's hospitals and genomic labs, and it offers a service model where clinicians upload patient exomes for AI-assisted diagnosis.

Malmo-based pharma company developing Orviglance, an oral manganese-based contrast agent for liver MRI scans, aimed at patients with kidney problems who cannot be given gadolinium agents. Listed on Nasdaq Stockholm. Pre-revenue and moving towards a US regulatory filing. Specialist hospital product with no consumer brand. The drug has completed a pivotal Phase 3 study, and the company plans a US filing with plans to partner for commercialisation.

Tampere-based orthopaedic implant company producing RemeOs, a bioresorbable metal screw and implants that dissolve in the body, eliminating removal surgery for fractures, and older polymer implants. Listed on Nasdaq First North Finland. Customers are hospitals and surgeons; revenue is small. B2B medical device brand with no consumer awareness. Its products are CE-marked, and the company has a US pathway for its flagship implants, with sales via distributors in Europe and Asia.

Korean biotechnology and pharmaceutical company based in Seoul, with a listed-company flag and a large funding figure in Korean won dated April 2026. The input gives no description of its products, pipeline, ownership or size. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

Korean biopharma company based in Pohang, with a large funding figure in Korean won dated August 2026 and a listed-company flag. The input offers no description of its products, pipeline or size. The name may refer to a hemp or cannabinoid business, but this cannot be confirmed. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

Alesund company that processes salmon by-products into protein hydrolysate (ProGo), omega-3 oil and calcium for dietary supplements, sports nutrition, pet food and joint-health products, sold as ingredients to food and supplement brands. Listed on Euronext Growth Oslo. Revenue comes from ingredient sales and some own products. B2B ingredients maker with limited consumer awareness. Fish processing by-products come from partner salmon farms, which reduces waste and gives the company a sustainability angle.

Gothenburg drug developer working on Parkinson's disease treatments, notably mesdopetam for levodopa-induced dyskinesia and pirepemat for falls, with a collaboration with Ipsen. Listed on Nasdaq Stockholm. Pre-revenue, with income from partner payments. Specialist neurology company with no consumer brand. The company emerged from research linked to Nobel laureate Arvid Carlsson, with a small team based in Gothenburg and income from its partnership.

Swedish cancer drug developer with fostroxacitabine bralpamide (fostrox), a liver-targeted nucleoside prodrug for liver cancer, plus partnered legacy products. Listed on Nasdaq Stockholm. Revenue is small. Specialist oncology company with no consumer brand. It is based in the Stockholm area and has a history in antivirals, before shifting to cancer research, with income from partner royalties, milestone payments and grants.

Israeli medical device company behind GelrinC, a biodegradable hydrogel implant that is injected into damaged knee cartilage and cured with UV light to support regrowth of cartilage, tested in clinical trials in Europe and the US. Venture-backed, based in Or Akiva near Haifa. Pre-revenue or early revenue, with no consumer brand awareness. The implant is positioned as an alternative to microfracture surgery and cartilage grafting for people with cartilage defects in the knee.

Lund biotech developing mitazalimab, a CD40 agonist antibody for pancreatic cancer and other cancers, partnered in Europe with Orion, plus earlier antibody programmes. Listed on Nasdaq Stockholm. Revenue comes from licence payments. Specialist oncology company with no consumer brand. The company was founded in 2000, and its antibody work stems from academic research in Lund, with a lean organisation and partners funding late-stage trials.

Dublin-registered pharma group with operations in Italy and Switzerland, known for the Winlevi (clascoterone) acne cream marketed by Sun Pharma in the US, GI Genius, an AI polyp-detection endoscopy system distributed by Medtronic, and gastro drugs such as Lialda and Uceris. Revenue comes from product sales, licences and royalties. Listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange (COPN). B2B pharma brand, with no direct consumer awareness.

Seoul genomic analysis company that provides sequencing, bioinformatics and personalised genetic testing services to hospitals, pharma and consumers, including cancer and rare disease panels and ancestry-type tests. Listed on KOSDAQ. Revenue comes from testing and analysis fees. Moderately known in Korean genomics circles, with some consumer-facing products. It was founded as a spin-off of Korean genomics research and has built its own sequencing lab, which generates data for pharmaceutical research.

Oslo cancer drug developer with LTX-315, a short peptide injected into tumours to trigger immune responses, and LTX-401 for liver tumours, built on discoveries from the University of Tromso. Listed on Euronext Growth Oslo. Pre-revenue, with partnerships and grants. No consumer brand. Its peptides are designed to kill cancer cells and prompt the immune system to attack remaining tumours, and have been tested in several solid tumour trials in Europe.

Swedish medical technology company with Nevisense, a hand-held device that uses electrical impedance spectroscopy to help dermatologists assess melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer, plus atopic dermatitis testing. Listed on Nasdaq Stockholm. Revenue is small. Specialist B2B medical device brand with no consumer awareness. Its device is sold to dermatologists and clinics in Europe, with US regulatory approval, and revenue comes from device sales and per-use electrodes.

Korean biotech with drug candidates for atopic dermatitis (NuGel) and respiratory disease, and an immune-cell programme for COVID-19 pneumonia. Listed on KOSDAQ. Pre-revenue. Specialist drug developer with no consumer brand. The company has cut across several fields in immunology, and runs on research funding, partner payments and share issues, with a small research team. Revenue is minimal and spending on trials is funded through share offerings.

Israeli clinical-stage company developing SIL-204, an siRNA drug targeting KRAS mutations, delivered locally to tumours in pancreatic cancer. It became listed on Nasdaq in 2024 via a SPAC merger with Moringa. Pre-revenue. Specialist oncology company with no consumer brand. The company's drug is designed to switch off the mutant KRAS gene in pancreatic tumour cells, and a Phase 2/3 trial is planned. It has a small team and relies on share issues.

Israeli dermatology company with Twyneo (tretinoin and benzoyl peroxide) for acne and Epsolay (benzoyl peroxide cream) for rosacea, both using its microencapsulation platform, licensed to partners such as Galderma in the US and elsewhere. Based in Ness Ziona and listed on Nasdaq (SLGL). Revenue comes from partner milestones and royalties. Prescription-only dermatology brand with little consumer recognition. It has product lines in acne and rosacea and a separate programme for a rare skin disease, with development and manufacturing in Israel.

Atlanta biopharma company with GENOSYL DS, a delivery system for inhaled nitric oxide approved by the FDA for newborns with hypoxic respiratory failure and used in hospital intensive care units, designed to be easier to handle than gas cylinder systems. Customers are hospitals. Venture-backed, with a major round in 2024. Specialist B2B hospital brand with no consumer awareness. The company is led from Atlanta, and the nitric oxide device is designed to be portable and easier to store.

about: Specialty pharmaceutical company that developed BELBUCA, a buprenorphine film for chronic pain, and BUNAVAIL for opioid dependence, using its film delivery technology. Customers were pain specialists and pharmacies, with revenue of around 100 million dollars. Listed on Nasdaq (BDSI). Collegium Pharmaceutical acquired it in 2022 for about 604 million dollars. Prescription brand with no consumer profile. BDSI was headquartered in Raleigh and built its business around films that dissolve in the mouth, a niche in pain and addiction treatment.

Biotechnology and health care company from Dundee, Scotland, which Crunchbase says develops oral therapies, with a funding figure of about 202 million dollars dated June 2025. The input does not detail its products, trial stage, owners or size, and the funding figure appears large for a small firm. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: Strasbourg-area biotech developing viral-vector immunotherapies against cancer, including TG4050, a personalised neoantigen vaccine, and TG6002, an oncolytic virus. Majority-owned by Institut Merieux, listed on Euronext Paris (TNG). Revenue is small, mostly collaboration income. Specialist oncology company with no consumer brand. It is a part of the Merieux group of French healthcare investors and also works with partners on vaccine candidates for cancers.

Biopharmaceutical firm from Marseille, tagged under biotechnology and oncology, with a funding figure of about 135 million dollars dated October 2025. The name suggests antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) for cancer. The input does not name any lead drug, investors or ownership. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: Swedish clinical-stage biotech developing TCR-T cell therapies, including a programme aimed at mutant KRAS-driven cancers, with the first trial called VISION in pancreatic cancer. Based in Sodertalje. Venture-funded. Pre-revenue and research-focused, with no consumer brand. The company plans to run trials in Europe, with hospitals as the likely customers, and relies on investors for funding while it is pre-revenue. It has had European research funding.
cb_desc: Anocca is aclinical-stage biopharmaceutical company...

about: San Diego biopharmaceutical company (Nasdaq: ACAD) focused on neurology and rare disease. Its products are Nuplazid for hallucinations and delusions in Parkinson's disease psychosis and Daybue, approved in 2023 as the first drug for Rett syndrome. Revenue from sales is more than 500 million dollars a year, sold through specialty pharmacies to neurologists and psychiatrists in the US, with Europe expansion. Founded 1993. B2B and patient-focused healthcare brand with minimal general consumer awareness.

Cambridge, Massachusetts biopharmaceutical company (Nasdaq: AGIO) focused on cellular metabolism and rare blood disorders. Its marketed drug is Pyrukynd (mitapivat) for hemolytic anemia in pyruvate kinase deficiency, being studied in thalassemia and sickle cell disease. It sold its oncology business, including Tibsovo, to Servier in 2021 for around 1.8 billion dollars. Sells to haematologists through specialty distribution in the US and Europe. B2B healthcare, little general public brand awareness.

San Francisco gene therapy developer that built adeno-associated virus treatments for rare neuromuscular diseases, led by AT132 for X-linked myotubular myopathy and programmes in Pompe disease and other disorders. It operated its own gene therapy manufacturing in North Carolina and was listed on Nasdaq (BOLD). Astellas acquired it in early 2020 for roughly 3 billion dollars. Clinical-stage, no marketed products at the time, and no consumer profile.

Redwood City medical robotics company that developed the Monarch platform, a flexible robotic endoscopy system for bronchoscopy to reach early lung nodules and for urology procedures, sold to hospitals. Johnson & Johnson acquired it in 2019 in a deal worth up to 5.75 billion dollars, and it operates inside J&J MedTech's robotics business. Its customers are hospitals and physicians rather than the public, so it has low consumer awareness.

Cambridge, Massachusetts epigenetics-focused drug developer, whose lead candidate pelabresib (CPI-0610) was being developed for myelofibrosis, a rare blood cancer. It listed on Nasdaq (CNST) in 2018 and was acquired by German biotech MorphoSys in 2021 for about 1.7 billion dollars; MorphoSys was then bought by Novartis in 2024. Clinical-stage biotech, so B2B only with no consumer presence. Its pelabresib programme targeted bromodomain (BET) inhibition, and the deal was driven by the late-stage MANIFEST-2 data.

Cambridge, Massachusetts biopharmaceutical company (Nasdaq: EPZM) that developed Tazverik (tazemetostat), a first-in-class EZH2 inhibitor approved for epithelioid sarcoma and relapsed follicular lymphoma, sold to oncologists in the US. Revenue was modest, around 30 to 40 million dollars. Ipsen acquired Epizyme in 2022 for roughly 247 million dollars plus a contingent value right. Oncology specialist with no consumer awareness. Tazverik was the first approved drug in its class and was launched in 2020, but sales remained limited and the company relied on partners in Japan and Greater China.

New Jersey oncology biotech that developed Trodelvy (sacituzumab govitecan), an antibody-drug conjugate for triple-negative breast cancer and other solid tumours, approved by the FDA in 2020. It was listed on Nasdaq (IMMU). Gilead acquired it in October 2020 for roughly 21 billion dollars, and Trodelvy is now one of Gilead's growth drugs, with annual sales above 1 billion dollars. B2B pharma, no consumer awareness.

Medical device company focused on extremity orthopaedics (foot and ankle, shoulder, upper limb) and biologics, with products such as total ankle replacements and shoulder systems sold to hospitals and surgeons. Formed from Wright Medical Group and Tornier, with a Memphis operational base, and listed on Nasdaq (WMGI). Stryker acquired it in November 2020 for around 5.4 billion dollars. B2B med-tech, no general consumer visibility.

Cambridge, Massachusetts gene therapy company created in a spin-off from Switzerland-based Ferring Pharmaceuticals to commercialise nadofaragene firadenovec, sold as Adstiladrin, a gene therapy for BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer that the FDA approved in 2022. Customers are urologists and hospitals. Privately held and backed by Ferring and investors, so B2B with minimal public brand recognition. The bladder cancer market is large, with several hundred thousand patients living with the disease in the US, and the therapy is delivered by instillation into the bladder in the urologist's office.

about: Guobang Pharma is a Chinese company in Hangzhou, Zhejiang, focused on pharmaceutical research, development and manufacturing, according to the input. No product names, customers or scale can be confirmed. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: Boston-area biotechnology company (Nasdaq: IRWD) whose main product is Linzess (linaclotide) for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and chronic constipation, which it sells in the US with AbbVie and licensed to partners in Asia and Europe. It generates several hundred million dollars from royalties and profit share. Spun off Cyclerion in 2019 and founded in 1998. Linzess is widely advertised to consumers.

Chinese pharmacy chain operator based in Changsha, Hunan, running thousands of company-owned and franchised drugstores across many provinces, selling prescription and over-the-counter drugs, health products and offering online pharmacy services. Listed in Shanghai, it is among China's largest drugstore chains by store count. Brand recognition is strong among consumers in central and southern China. The company sells through its store network under the Laobaixing name and also runs wholesale and online channels, with an estimated annual revenue in the tens of billions of yuan.
cb_desc: LBX Pharmacy is a discount pharmacy superstore chain.

about: Cambridge, Massachusetts biotechnology company (Nasdaq: MACK) that developed Onivyde, a liposomal irinotecan for pancreatic cancer, which it sold to Ipsen in 2017, before shrinking and winding down its drug pipeline and operations. It was founded in 2000 around network biology. Today it has little or no operations, so there is no meaningful sponsorship or consumer profile. It returned cash to shareholders after the asset sale and kept only a small research pipeline.

Massachusetts medical device maker of proton therapy systems for cancer, notably the compact single-room Mevion S250 and S250i with HYPERSCAN pencil beam scanning, sold to hospitals and cancer centres in the US and abroad. Its systems are cheaper and smaller than conventional cyclotron installations. Privately held with institutional investors. B2B with little general consumer awareness. It was founded in 2004 as Still River Systems, a spin-off from MIT-linked research, and sells to US hospitals and cancer centres.

about: Redwood City biopharmaceutical company that developed Veltassa (patiromer), a potassium binder for hyperkalemia in patients with kidney and heart disease, sold to nephrologists and cardiologists. It listed on Nasdaq (RLYP) in 2013 and was acquired by Swiss company Galenica in 2016 for around 1.5 billion dollars, later part of Vifor Pharma and CSL. B2B healthcare, no consumer visibility. Veltassa sold through hospital pharmacies and retail channels, and annual revenues were in the low hundreds of millions of dollars after launch.

Biopharmaceutical company focused on cancer immunotherapy, developing PD-L1 antibody envafolimab (KN035) with Alphamab and other oncology candidates, with operations in China and a US presence. It sells to hospitals and oncologists, with licensing and regional commercial agreements. It is privately held with venture backing. Clinical-stage and early commercial, so B2B with no consumer awareness. Its US base in Fremont, California supports clinical trials and business development for Western markets, while commercial sales are driven mostly through Chinese partners.

about: California neurology-focused pharma company (Nasdaq: ADMS) that sold Gocovri (extended-release amantadine) for dyskinesia in Parkinson's disease and Osmolex ER, using proprietary controlled-release technology. Customers are neurologists in the US through specialty channels. Acquired in November 2021 by Supernus Pharmaceuticals for roughly 400 million dollars. B2B healthcare, no consumer brand awareness. Gocovri was the first drug approved specifically for dyskinesia in Parkinson's, and Adamas was founded in 2000 in the San Francisco Bay Area.

California biotech (Nasdaq: AIMT) that launched Palforzia, the first FDA-approved treatment for peanut allergy in children, based on controlled oral immunotherapy, sold through allergists. Nestlé Health Science acquired Aimmune in 2020 for around 2.6 billion dollars, and Palforzia now sits within Nestlé. Customers are allergists, hospitals and families with allergic children, so brand awareness is moderate in niche circles. Palforzia's launch in 2020 was hit by COVID-19 and slow patient uptake, but the product remained a first-in-class treatment, with peanut allergy affecting roughly 1-2% of children.

Waltham, Massachusetts clinical-stage biopharma that uses an AI and multi-omics platform built on patient biology to discover drugs and biomarkers, with candidates including BPM31510 for glioblastoma and pancreatic cancer. It grew out of Berg and works with academic and industry partners. Privately held and venture-backed, B2B with no consumer profile. Its approach combines patient tissue samples, mass spectrometry data and artificial intelligence to identify disease mechanisms, rather than one single product.

about: Cambridge, Massachusetts clinical-stage immuno-oncology company (Nasdaq: GNCA) developing neoantigen cancer vaccines (GEN-009) and checkpoint-related therapies, using a platform for identifying T-cell targets. It ran early clinical trials and had pharma partnerships, but struggled to fund development and went through bankruptcy and liquidation in 2022. B2B biotech with no consumer profile. Genocea was founded in 2007 in Cambridge and went public in 2014, with a platform called ATLAS used for identifying antigens from tumour samples.

about: Cambridge, Massachusetts oncology drug developer (Nasdaq: INFI) whose main product was Copiktra (duvelisib), a PI3K inhibitor for blood cancers licensed to Secura Bio, plus other PI3K-gamma candidates such as eganelisib. Revenues came from licensing and royalties, not product sales. It filed for Chapter 11 in 2023 as funding ran out. B2B biotech, no consumer visibility. Copiktra was approved in 2018 and commercialised by Verastem and later Secura Bio, with Infinity receiving milestones and royalties.

about: Flagship Pioneering company in Cambridge, Massachusetts developing therapeutics based on engineered circular RNA (eRNA), an RNA drug platform with long-lasting expression. It raised significant venture funding and was renamed Sail Biomedicines in 2022. Pre-clinical or early stage, so it works with research and pharma partners rather than consumers, and has no consumer awareness. Flagship incubated it in stealth and launched it publicly in 2021, making the circular RNA platform one of the better funded in biotech.

Palo Alto software company whose cloud platform runs decentralised clinical trials, remote patient data capture, electronic consent and AI-assisted trial tools for pharmaceutical companies, CROs and academic centres. It raised hundreds of millions of dollars, with a valuation above 2 billion dollars in 2021. Revenue comes from subscriptions and services. B2B, little awareness outside life sciences. Its tools cover patient apps, video visits and e-consent for people taking part in trials, rather than treating them, and have been used by large pharma sponsors.

Biopharmaceutical company that developed Orgovyx (relugolix) for advanced prostate cancer and Myfembree for uterine fibroids and endometriosis pain, selling to urologists and gynaecologists in the US. It was majority-owned by Sumitomo Pharma and listed on the NYSE (MYOV) before being taken fully into Sumitomo in 2023 for roughly 1.7 billion dollars. B2B, with patient-facing marketing for women's health. Myfembree was co-commercialised with Pfizer, and Orgovyx was the first oral GnRH antagonist for prostate cancer, offering an alternative to injections.

San Diego biotech (Nasdaq: OTIC) that developed drugs for ear disorders, including the marketed Otiprio antibiotic gel for middle ear infections and pipeline treatments for hearing loss and tinnitus. It sold to ear, nose and throat specialists in the US. After clinical setbacks it wound down and dissolved around 2023. No consumer visibility. Otonomy was founded in 2008 and listed on Nasdaq in 2014, and its pipeline included OTO-413 and OTO-313 for hearing loss and tinnitus, which did not succeed.

about: Irish neuroscience company (Nasdaq: PRTA), spun out of Elan, developing antibody immunotherapies against protein misfolding diseases, including birtamimab for AL amyloidosis and programmes in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's with partners such as Novo Nordisk and Roche. It receives collaboration and royalty revenue, with no marketed product of its own. B2B clinical-stage biotech, no consumer awareness. Prothena was formed in 2012 and operates from Dublin and South San Francisco, and its shares trade on Nasdaq with a market value in the low billions of dollars.

Beijing vaccine maker (Nasdaq: SVA) best known for CoronaVac, an inactivated COVID-19 vaccine used in China and shipped to dozens of countries such as Indonesia, Brazil and Turkey. Other products include hepatitis A (Healive), EV71 and varicella vaccines. Revenue peaked in 2021 and fell afterwards, with management disputes. Known through the pandemic to the public, but largely B2B government sales.

Chinese-founded clinical trial technology company with a US office, offering cloud-based electronic data capture and clinical trial management software, randomisation and supply tools to pharmaceutical firms and contract research organisations in China and abroad. Revenue comes from software subscriptions and services. B2B life-sciences software with no consumer awareness. The platform is used by pharma sponsors, hospitals and CROs to run trials efficiently, with customers mainly among Chinese drug developers, and the company also sells to global sponsors.

about: Maryland biotechnology company (Nasdaq: VIE), formerly spun out of AstraZeneca and MedImmune, that developed Uplizna (inebilizumab) for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, an autoimmune neurological disease, sold to neurologists. Horizon Therapeutics acquired it in 2021 for roughly 3 billion dollars, and Amgen later bought Horizon in 2023. B2B, no consumer visibility. Uplizna was approved by the FDA in June 2020 and later extended to IgG4-related disease, selling at a high price per infusion, with customers mostly academic and community neurologists.

Guangzhou-based B2B online platform for pharmaceutical trading, connecting drug wholesalers and manufacturers with small pharmacies and clinics, providing ordering, logistics and credit services. It serves independent drugstores in China and earns margin and service fees. A fast-growing digital health marketplace with strong recognition among pharmacy owners, but little among the public. It started around 2014 and has built a large network of independent drugstores as customers, making it a recognised digital supplier in China's pharmaceutical distribution.

about: Texas medical device company (Nasdaq: APEN) focused on obesity treatments, notably the Orbera intragastric balloon and the Lap-Band adjustable gastric band, sold to bariatric surgeons and clinics in the US and abroad. Boston Scientific acquired it in 2023 for about 615 million dollars. B2B med-tech, though the Lap-Band name is known to patients. The business was a mid-sized medical devices firm with annual sales in the range of 70 million dollars, with Orbera and Lap-Band the biggest products.

Belgian molecular diagnostics company whose Idylla platform delivers rapid cancer genotyping and infectious disease tests from a small cartridge-based system, sold to hospitals and labs worldwide. It listed on Euronext Brussels in 2015 and ran into financial distress; the input flags the company as liquidated. B2B medical devices with no consumer awareness. Idylla tests are used to detect cancer mutations that decide on treatments for colorectal, lung and melanoma cancers, and the platform is used in labs in dozens of countries.
cb_desc: Public molecular diagnostics company -liquidated.

about: Biotechnology company with Chinese and US operations (Durham, North Carolina) developing treatments for infectious diseases including chronic hepatitis B and HIV, COVID-19 antibodies and other viral and CNS programmes. Listed in Hong Kong in 2021, it licenses and develops drugs across the US and China. Clinical-stage, so B2B with no consumer profile. It has significant operations in China (Beijing and Shanghai) and a US office in Durham, North Carolina.

about: Texas diagnostics company (Nasdaq: CSTL) known for DecisionDx-Melanoma, a gene expression profile test that estimates metastasis risk in skin cancer, plus tests for uveal melanoma, Barrett's oesophagus and dermatology conditions. Customers are physicians and pathologists, reimbursed by Medicare and private insurers, with revenue in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Founded 2007. B2B clinical lab, with little public awareness. The company's business revolves around skin cancer testing, which it can market directly to dermatologists and surgical oncologists, so it has built a focused sales force across the US.

Menlo Park drug delivery company (Nasdaq: CORI) that developed transdermal and transmucosal patches and sold contract manufacturing and licensed products such as the ADHD patch for Noven and others. Customers were large pharma partners. It was acquired in 2018 by Gurnet Point Capital and Juniper Pharmaceuticals for around 500 million dollars. B2B, no consumer brand. Its technology allowed delivery of drugs through the skin, which avoids pills, with patch manufacturing in Grand Rapids, Michigan.

about: Minnesota medical device company (Nasdaq: CVRX) selling the Barostim system, an implantable baroreflex activation therapy for patients with heart failure and resistant hypertension, to hospitals and cardiologists in the US and Europe. Revenue is tens of millions of dollars and growing. Founded in 2001. B2B medical technology, with little general consumer awareness. The system works like a pacemaker for blood pressure, with a pulse generator implanted below the collarbone and an electrode connected to the carotid sinus, and has FDA approval for heart failure since 2019.

Chinese biologics developer listed in Hong Kong that develops antibody drugs for cancer and autoimmune diseases, such as the PD-1 antibody geptanolimab and TNF-alpha antibody candidates. Customers are hospitals, with partnerships for rights in China and abroad. Revenue is small and losses persistent. B2B biotech with no consumer visibility. R&D and pilot manufacturing are based in China, and it listed in Hong Kong around 2020.
cb_desc: Genor Biopharma is a science- driven, inovative biologics...

about: California population genomics and health company that sequences customers' exomes through health systems, employers and research programmes and operates a genomic data marketplace for partners such as pharma and research institutions. It built tests, apps and clinical programmes with large backing from investors and partners including Illumina. B2B and B2B2C platform with limited consumer brand awareness. Its flagship product is the Helix Exome+ test, and it has partnered with health systems such as Mount Sinai and Geisinger to roll out population sequencing programmes.

about: Bermuda-incorporated, Massachusetts-based biopharmaceutical company (Nasdaq: KNSA) selling Arcalyst (rilonacept) for recurrent pericarditis, a rare heart inflammation, generating revenue of several hundred million dollars from specialist cardiologists and rheumatologists in the US. It also develops follow-on antibody therapies and obtained rights from Regeneron. B2B healthcare with no consumer awareness. Kiniksa was started by the Baker Bros investment group in 2015, and the company has little general brand visibility.

Cambridge, Massachusetts biotech developing antibody-drug conjugates and conditioning therapies to prepare patients for stem cell transplants, with candidates such as MGTA-117. It listed on Nasdaq (MGTA) in 2018 and merged with Dianthus Therapeutics in 2023 after cutting its programmes. Clinical-stage biotech, no consumer awareness. The company was founded in 2015, and raised funds from investors, while its shares fell sharply after trial data, leading to the merger with a private biotech and a reverse listing.
cb_desc: Magenta Therapeutics is a new biotechnology company...

about: New Jersey in vitro diagnostics company providing blood typing, immunoassay and clinical chemistry systems and reagents to hospitals, labs and blood banks in 125 countries. It was carved out of Johnson & Johnson by Carlyle in 2014, listed on Nasdaq (OCDX) in 2021 and merged with Quidel in 2022 to form QuidelOrtho. Revenue was about 2 billion dollars. B2B, no consumer visibility.

Boston company that pioneered prescription digital therapeutics, FDA-authorised software treatments such as reSET for substance use disorder (the first of its kind in 2017), reSET-O for opioid use disorder and Somryst for chronic insomnia. It sold to clinicians and payers and listed on Nasdaq (PEAR) through a 2021 SPAC merger. Slow insurer reimbursement led to a Chapter 11 filing in April 2023, and its assets were sold, including to Nox Health. Defunct as an independent business.

Newark, California clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company (Nasdaq: PTGX) built on peptide drug discovery. Its lead programmes are rusfertide, an injectable hepcidin mimetic for polycythemia vera developed with Takeda, and icotrokinra (JNJ-2113), an oral IL-23 receptor antagonist peptide partnered with Johnson & Johnson for psoriasis and ulcerative colitis. Revenue is collaboration and milestone based, so it has no marketed product of its own to patients yet. B2B biotech with no consumer brand.

Jiangsu-based vaccine developer, listed in Hong Kong, working on recombinant vaccines including a 9-valent HPV candidate, a recombinant shingles vaccine and adjuvant technology. It is still pre-revenue and relies on clinical trial progress in China. Customers will ultimately be Chinese provincial disease-control centres and private vaccination clinics. B2B life-science company with no consumer brand recognition yet. Its candidates compete with Merck's Gardasil and with HPV vaccines from domestic Chinese rivals.

about: Cambridge, Massachusetts biotech founded by Flagship Pioneering that tried to engineer red blood cells as a platform for cell therapies against cancer, autoimmune and rare disease. It listed on Nasdaq (RUBY) in 2018 and raised heavily from investors, but cut back after poor clinical progress and wound down operations in 2023. No marketed products and no consumer presence. Its approach, called Red Cell Therapeutics, used genetically engineered red cell precursors as carriers.

Lexington, Massachusetts messenger RNA therapeutics company that was developing treatments for cystic fibrosis (MRT5005) and for primary ciliary dyskinesia, and mRNA vaccine programmes in partnership with Sanofi. It listed on Nasdaq (TBIO) and was acquired by Sanofi in September 2021 for roughly 3.2 billion dollars to build Sanofi's mRNA centre of excellence. B2B biotech with no consumer profile. It also built mRNA manufacturing capacity in Massachusetts.

California medical technology company (Nasdaq: AFIB) selling the AcQMap high-resolution 3D cardiac imaging and mapping system for treating complex arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, as well as catheters and left-heart access tools.
